unit.title: Mark off/out structural fabrications and shapes

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: For the hole positions on one beam, which drawing should the marker work from?
options: The general arrangement of the whole building
The architect's sketch of the front view
The shop drawing for that beam's piece mark
The foundation drawing for the column bases

questions.stem: A beam drawing gives every bolt hole from the beam's centre line, not from its ends. Which line should be marked and checked first?
options: The centre line the sizes are taken from
A line along the bottom edge of the web
A line 100 mm in from the left-hand end
The line of the first hole shown

questions.stem: Why are bolt holes in a universal beam flange marked on two gauge lines, and not on the centre of the flange?
options: The flange is thinnest at its centre
Two lines are quicker to mark than one
The web is in the way at the centre
The code allows only two holes per flange

questions.stem: What is meant by the 'cross-centres' of bolt holes in a beam flange?
options: The distance from the first hole to the beam end
The gap between the two hole lines across the flange
The distance between any two holes along one hole line
The distance from the hole to the edge of the web

questions.stem: On an unequal angle, why does the drawing give a separate back mark for each leg?
options: One leg is always drilled and the other leg always welded
Each leg is a different width, so its hole line differs
The longer leg is always made from thicker steel
The back mark changes with the length of the angle

questions.stem: Holes 9 m apart are to be marked on a column. Why is the steel tape supported and pulled to a steady tension?
options: So the tape does not rust on the steel
So the hook does not scratch the paint
Sag and stretch change long readings
So the tape reads in inches as well

questions.stem: Before marking out, a channel is found to be twisted along its length. Why must this be found before any marks are made?
options: Marks squared from a twisted face end up out of place
Twisted steel cannot be painted after it is cut
A twisted channel is always too short for the job in hand
Twist makes the steel heavier to lift and turn

questions.stem: A drawing asks for a beam to be cambered 15 mm. What does this mean?
options: It is cut 15 mm longer than the drawing size
Its flanges are trimmed 15 mm narrower
It is curved up 15 mm at mid-span
Its end holes are moved 15 mm inwards

questions.stem: Why is a cope marked with a radius at its inside corner, and not a sharp square corner?
options: A radius is quicker to mark with a square
A sharp corner can start a crack
A radius makes the beam lighter to lift
Sharp corners cannot be flame cut at all

questions.stem: A beam is coped so it fits under the top flange of the beam that carries it. Which size mainly sets the depth of the cope?
options: The length of the coped beam itself
The width of the coped beam's own flange
The number of bolts used in the beam's end connection
The carrying beam's flange and root, plus clearance

questions.stem: Why are the inside corners of web stiffener plates marked with a small cut-off (a snipe)?
options: To make each stiffener plate easier to lift by hand
To clear the root radius and the flange-to-web weld
To save steel on every stiffener plate cut
To show the welder which side is the front

questions.stem: Why is a roof truss often set out full size on a flat floor or plate table before the members are cut?
options: To find true lengths and angles, and use it as a jig
So the client can walk round it before it is all built
Because truss drawings never give any sizes
So the members can be cut by eye from the lines

questions.stem: On a full-size truss layout, the centre lines of three members meet at one point. What is this point usually called?
options: A witness mark on the steel
A back mark
A datum edge
A node, or working point

questions.stem: A roof truss has a span of 8 m and a rise of 1.5 m at the centre. About how long is each rafter centre line, from the eaves node to the apex?
A rafter is pitched at 15°. The half span is 6 m. Using tan 15° = 0.268, what is the rise at the apex?
Why might a cutting list add a small shrinkage allowance to the length of a heavily welded built-up column?
options: Paint adds a little length to the column
Welds shrink as they cool and shorten it
The saw blade always cuts a little long
Steel stretches in the sun on site

questions.stem: A 6 mm plate is bent to a 90° angle with outside legs of 100 mm and 100 mm. Why is the flat blank shorter than 200 mm?
options: The outside stretches, so a shorter blank is enough
The press brake cuts a little off each end
The plate gets thinner all over when it is bent
The 6 mm thickness is taken off each of the legs twice

questions.stem: A cylinder with an inside diameter of 1 000 mm is rolled from 10 mm plate. Using the mean diameter and π = 3.142, about what plate length is needed?
Which method of development is used to mark out an oblique cone, whose apex is not straight above the centre of its base?
options: Radial line from the apex
Triangulation
Parallel line
A simple stretch-out of the base circle

questions.stem: When a square-to-round transition is developed by triangulation, what must be found for each line before it is drawn on the pattern?
options: Its true length
Its plan length only
Its weight in kilograms
Its angle to the floor

questions.stem: How is the true length of a sloping line found from its plan length and its height?
options: Add the plan length and the height together, then halve it
Draw a right-angled triangle of plan length and height
Double the plan length and ignore the height
Take the height away from the plan length

questions.stem: A 100 mm pipe branch meets a 150 mm main at 90°, with their centre lines meeting. Which method develops the shape of the branch end?
options: Radial line development
Triangulation from the main
Parallel line development
A straight cut at 45°

questions.stem: A 90° lobster-back bend has two full segments and two half segments, so it has three joints. At what angle from square is each end of a full segment cut?
Why is a wrap-around template for a pipe branch marked with the pipe's quarter lines?
options: So it lines up with the quarter marks on the pipe
So it can be folded into four for storage
So the welder knows where to start welding
So it shows the pipe's wall thickness

questions.stem: Holes in a splice plate must line up exactly with holes in a beam flange. Which method best makes sure of this?
options: Mark each part by eye from the drawing
Mark both from one template, or drill them together
Mark the plate, then open up any hole that is found out
Mark the beam on site after it is erected

questions.stem: Why must the edge distance of each bolt hole be checked against the drawing?
options: Too small a distance can let the bolt tear out
Edge distance decides the colour of the paint
A larger edge distance makes the bolt shorter
Edge distance matters only on aluminium

questions.stem: Bolt holes on two gauge lines are said to be 'staggered'. What does this mean?
options: The holes are of different sizes on each line
Holes on one line sit midway between those on the other
The holes are drilled at a slant right through the steel
The second line of holes is drilled on site

questions.stem: A beam's length tolerance is ±2 mm. Your cut line gives a length 2.5 mm over size. What should you do?
options: Cut it, as 2.5 mm is close enough
Cut it, and grind the end on site if needed
Re-mark it within tolerance before it is cut
Cut it 5 mm short to be safe

questions.stem: A column base plate must fit anchor bolts already cast into concrete on site. How is its hole pattern best checked?
options: Trust the foundation drawing and drill from it
Make the holes 20 mm oversize to be safe
Make a template from the cast-in bolts and compare
Slot every hole so it can be moved later

questions.stem: A beam on trestles must be turned over so its other flange can be marked. What is the safest method?
options: Two people roll it over with bars
Use a crane or turning aid in a planned lift
Lever it off the trestles onto the floor
Push it over and let it fall onto old tyres

questions.stem: A beam is hanging from the shop crane so that its underside can be marked. What should be done?
options: Mark it quickly while it hangs
Have one person steady it by hand
Lower it onto stands before marking
Stand beside it, not under it, to mark

questions.stem: Why are the trestles used for marking heavy beams checked for their safe working load?
options: An overloaded trestle can collapse
Heavy beams scratch the trestle paint
The trestles must match the beam size
Light trestles are harder to move

questions.stem: Which tool is best for carrying a level datum line round a large built-up column standing in the shop?
options: A short spirit level and a pencil
A laser level or a water level
A tape measure from the floor at each face
A plumb bob hung from the top

questions.stem: Which tool is best for setting out a cut line at a set angle across a beam flange, such as for a skew cut?
options: A centre punch and a hammer
A pair of odd-leg calipers
A chalk line snapped along the web
A sliding bevel set with a protractor

questions.stem: Seen in plan, a beam meets a column face at 60°, not square. How many degrees from square is the cut line on the beam end?
A wrap-around template is to be made for pipe of 168.3 mm outside diameter. Using π = 3.142, how long must its stretch-out line be, to the nearest mm?
options: 505 mm
538 mm
561 mm
529 mm

questions.stem: A length of angle is to be bent round a 90° corner by cutting a V-notch out of one leg. What angle is the V-notch?
Why are the bevel line on the plate face and the root face line on the edge marked before a weld preparation is cut?
options: So the cut gives the angle and root face the WPS needs
So the welder can weld it without ever reading the WPS
So the plate can be cut without any guide
So the inspector can see where to grind

questions.stem: When a batch of 12 rafters is marked out, what is a 'first-off' check?
options: A check of the last rafter only
A full check of the first one before the rest
Checking that the first rafter is painted
Taking the first rafter off the trestles

questions.stem: You lead three markers working on 40 cleats and 12 beams. How can you be sure every hole pattern is checked?
options: Each marker checks his own work by eye
Check only the beams, as cleats are small
A second person checks each and signs a check sheet
The erectors check the holes on site when they bolt up

questions.stem: Why should the marking-out check sheet record which tape or rule was used?
options: So a faulty tape can be traced to its parts
So the tape can be returned to the store
So the client knows the tape's brand
So the marker can claim the tape's cost

questions.stem: While marking, you see that two beams on the drawing would clash at a connection. What should you do?
options: Move the holes where you think best
Cut both beams shorter to make room
Mark it as drawn; the erectors will sort it
Stop and send a query to the drawing office

questions.stem: Why are gusset plates for a welded truss often marked straight from the full-size layout?
options: Gussets are never shown on the drawing
It avoids having to cut the gussets
Their shapes and angles come from the true layout
So any size of plate can be used

questions.stem: An angle is 1.8 m long. The first and last holes are 40 mm from the ends, with 5 equal spaces between holes. What is the pitch?
options: 344 mm
352 mm
360 mm

questions.stem: A full-size truss layout on the shop floor is no longer needed. What should be done before it is cleaned off?
options: Clean it off at once to free the floor
Leave it for the next job to use
Paint over it so it cannot be seen
Check the batch is complete and record the layout sizes

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name for the sideways bow in a beam or column, seen when looking down on it from above?
What is the name for a pipe bend made from short, mitred pieces of straight pipe welded together?
A brace rises 1.2 m over a run of 1.6 m. How long is the brace, in metres?
What is the name for the painted code, such as B12, that tells the erector which piece goes where?
Holes are at 70 mm pitch on each of two staggered gauge lines. Measured along the member, how far in mm is a hole on one line from the next hole on the other line?
The stretch-out of a pipe template is 528 mm long and is to be split into 12 equal parts. How long is each part, in mm?
A line has a plan length of 400 mm and a height of 300 mm. What is its true length, in mm?
A lobster-back bend is made of three full segments and two half segments. How many segment joints (welds) does it have?
What is the name of the shape left when a cone has its top cut off parallel to its base?
What is the name of the drawing of the whole structure that shows where each piece mark goes?
Nine holes are in a line at 75 mm pitch. What is the distance, in mm, from the centre of the first hole to the centre of the last?
What is the name for an opening cut in a beam web, often round, to let a pipe or duct pass through?
A truss has a span of 12 m and a pitch of 1 in 4 (a rise of 1 m for each 4 m of run). What is the rise at the apex, in metres?
What is the name of the line inside a bent plate that keeps its length while the outside stretches and the inside is squeezed?
Which development method uses lines that all come from one point, the apex, to mark out a right cone?

essays.stem: You lead a team marking out the steel for a small portal frame (two columns, two rafters, haunches and base plates). Explain how you would plan the job, check the drawings and steel, and share the work.
essays.modelAnswer: I first check that I have the latest shop drawings and the general arrangement, and that the revisions match. I read every piece mark and make a cutting list with lengths, holes and any copes or haunch plates. I check the steel delivered against the list: section size, grade, length, and that it is straight, with no sweep, twist or damage. I check the tapes, squares and levels. I plan the order: base plates and column caps first, then the columns and rafters, which take longer. I share the work by skill: one person marks plates from templates, two mark the columns and rafters together, and I check. A first-off of each piece is fully checked against the drawing before the rest. A second person checks every piece and signs the check sheet. Each piece is painted with its mark. Queries go to the drawing office before cutting.
markingPoints: Latest drawings and revisions; cutting list made
Checks steel size, grade, length and straightness
Checks tools and plans the order of work
Shares work by skill; first-off checks
Second-person check, piece marks, queries raised

essays.stem: Explain how you would mark out the bolt holes in the flanges and web of a universal beam end connection, including gauge lines, cross-centres, pitch, end and edge distances, and how you would check them.
essays.modelAnswer: I set the beam on level trestles and check it for sweep and twist. I mark a square line across both flanges and the web at the datum the drawing uses, usually the end or the centre line of the beam. For the flange holes I mark the gauge lines either side of the web, using the cross-centres from the drawing, measured from the centre of the flange so both lines are even. For the web holes I mark a centre line on the web and the hole lines from it. Along each line I mark the end distance to the first hole, then each pitch, measured from the datum and not hole to hole, so errors do not add up. I check the edge distance of each hole. I centre punch lightly, check every size again against the drawing, then punch fully and mark a circle round each. A second person checks and signs.
markingPoints: Beam set up and checked; square datum line on all faces
Gauge lines from the flange centre at the cross-centres
Web centre line and hole lines
End distance and pitch from the datum; edge distance checked
Light punch, recheck, punch, second-person check

essays.stem: Describe how to mark out a cope on a beam end that fits into a supporting beam, and the web stiffeners on the supporting beam, explaining the radius and the snipes.
essays.modelAnswer: For the cope I take the sizes from the supporting beam: the depth is its flange thickness and root radius plus a small clearance, and the length is half its flange width plus a clearance, unless the drawing gives sizes. I mark a square line across the top flange and web of the coped beam at the cope length, then mark the cope depth down the web. At the inside corner I mark a radius, often about 10 to 15 mm, or as the drawing says, because a sharp corner can start a crack. I show the waste side clearly. For each stiffener I measure the clear distance between the flanges of the supporting beam and half the flange width minus half the web. I mark the outline and cut off the inside corners at an angle, the snipes, so the stiffener clears the root radius and the flange-to-web weld. I mark the stiffener positions on the web from the drawing.
markingPoints: Cope sizes from the supporting beam plus clearance
Square lines, cope depth and waste side marked
Inside radius and why
Stiffener sizes from the beam dimensions
Snipes to clear the root radius and weld; positions marked

essays.stem: Describe how to set out a roof truss full size on the shop floor or plate table from a drawing, and how the layout is used to mark and check the members and gussets.
essays.modelAnswer: I clean the floor or table and check it is flat. I snap a straight base line for the bottom chord and mark its centre. I work out the rafter length from the span and rise, and mark the apex by striking arcs of the rafter length from each eaves node, using trammels or a tape, then check the height. I draw the centre lines of all members and mark each node. I check the layout by measuring the diagonals and comparing both halves. Then I mark the member outlines, such as the back of each angle, from the setting-out lines. I lay each piece of steel on the layout to mark its cut lines and angles, so every member fits at the nodes. I make gusset templates straight from the layout, with the members' positions on them. I add stops or tacks so the layout can be used as a jig, and record the sizes.
markingPoints: Flat surface; base line and centre marked
Apex found by arcs from rafter length; height checked
Centre lines and nodes drawn; layout checked
Members laid on layout to mark cuts and angles
Gusset templates from layout; used as a jig; sizes recorded

essays.stem: A pitched roof truss has a span of 10 m and a rise of 2 m. Show how to work out the length of each rafter on its centre line, and explain the other allowances needed before the cut length is marked.
essays.modelAnswer: Each rafter covers half the span, which is 10 ÷ 2 = 5 m, and rises 2 m. The rafter centre line is the long side of a right-angled triangle, so its length is the square root of 5² + 2². That is the square root of 25 + 4 = 29, which is about 5.385 m, or 5 385 mm. This is the length from node to node on the centre line. It is not yet the cut length. At the apex the two rafters meet, so each end is cut back to the angle and to the joint detail, for example the gap or the plate between them. At the eaves the rafter end is cut to fit the bottom chord or seat plate. Any overhang at the eaves is added. If the truss is welded, a small allowance for shrinkage may be added. I check the final cut length against the full-size layout before cutting.
markingPoints: Half span 5 m and rise 2 m in a right-angled triangle
Correct working: √(25 + 4) = √29
Answer about 5.385 m node to node
Explains end cuts at apex and eaves, and overhang
Shrinkage allowance and checking against the layout

essays.stem: A hopper outlet needs a square-to-round transition with its round top set off to one side. Explain how you would develop its pattern by triangulation, and how you would check the pattern before marking steel.
essays.modelAnswer: I draw the plan full size, with the square and the circle in their true places, the circle set off to one side as the drawing gives, and an elevation showing the height. I divide the circle into equal parts, usually 12, and join each point to the nearest corner of the square, so the surface is split into flat triangles and curved corner sections. Because the top is off-centre, the lines on each side are different, so every line needs its own true length. For each one I draw a right-angled triangle with its plan length as the base and the height as the upright; the sloping side is the true length. I write them in a table. I build the pattern from the seam line, one triangle at a time, using the true lengths and the true spaces along the square and round the circle. To check it, I cut the pattern in card, bend it up and see that it closes, the top is round and the base square, before marking steel.
markingPoints: Plan and elevation with the offset; circle divided equally
Points joined to corners to form triangles
Every line needs its own true length because of the offset
True length by right-angled triangle; table kept
Pattern built from the seam; checked with a card model before marking

essays.stem: Describe how to set out and mark a three-joint 90° lobster-back bend on pipe, including the segment angles and the template.
essays.modelAnswer: A three-joint 90° bend has two half segments at the ends and two full segments in the middle. The bend turns 90° over three joints, so each joint turns 30°, and each cut face is 15° from square. I draw a side view with the bend radius from the drawing and mark the joint lines, then draw the pipe's outside diameter. For the template I draw the end view of the pipe, divide it into 12 equal parts and project them onto the side view of one half segment. I draw a stretch-out line equal to the pipe circumference and mark the 12 divisions along it. I carry each height from the side view to its division and join the points with a smooth curve. This curve is used for every cut. I mark quarter lines on the pipe, wrap the template on, line it up and scribe each cut, turning the template for opposite ends.
markingPoints: Two half and two full segments; 30° per joint, 15° per cut
Side view with bend radius and joint lines
End view divided and projected
Stretch-out of the circumference and the curve plotted
Quarter lines, template wrapped and scribed for each cut

essays.stem: A built-up welded plate girder 8 m long must finish within ±3 mm and have a 10 mm camber. Explain how you would allow for weld shrinkage and camber when marking out its web and flanges, and how you would check it.
essays.modelAnswer: Long welds along the web and flanges shrink as they cool, so the finished girder can be shorter, and it can bow. I find the shrinkage allowance from the shop's procedure or past jobs, and add it to the marked lengths of the web and flanges, or leave the ends long and trim them after welding. For the camber, I mark the web plate with a curved top and bottom edge, not straight. I set out a base line, mark stations along it, and at each station mark the camber offset so the curve rises to 10 mm at mid-span. The flanges are then fitted to the curved web. I check the camber again after welding with a string line or level at the stations, and the length against the ±3 mm tolerance before the ends are cut. I record the results on the check sheet.
markingPoints: Welds shrink and shorten or bow the girder
Adds shrinkage allowance or leaves ends long to trim
Marks the web with camber offsets at stations
Checks camber after welding with string line or level
Checks length within tolerance and records

essays.stem: Explain how marking-out errors on structural steel are prevented and found before cutting, including checks, tolerances, records and the role of a second checker.
essays.modelAnswer: Errors are prevented by using the latest drawings, checking that sizes add up, and querying anything unclear with the drawing office. Tools are checked before the job: tapes against a reference, squares against a master. Every size is measured from one datum, not from mark to mark, and long tapes are supported and pulled steadily. A first-off of each part is fully checked before the batch is marked. Before cutting, a second person checks each part against the drawing and the tolerances given, such as ±2 mm on length, and checks diagonals, hole patterns and copes. Both sign the check sheet, which records the piece mark, the tape used and any faults found. Parts outside tolerance are re-marked and the old marks cancelled clearly. If the same error keeps happening, the team leader finds the cause, such as a faulty tape or a misread drawing.
markingPoints: Latest drawings and queries raised
Tools checked; one datum; long tapes handled correctly
First-off check before the batch
Second person checks against tolerances and signs
Records kept; errors re-marked and causes found

essays.stem: Explain how you would check that the marked-out parts for a steel staircase (two stringers, treads and a landing frame) will fit together before they are cut, and what you would do if they would not.
essays.modelAnswer: I start from the drawing: the total rise, the total going, the number of steps and the rise and going of each step. I check these add up, for example that the number of rises times each rise equals the total rise. I work out the stringer length and angle from the total rise and going, and check it against a full-size set-out of the bottom and top of the stringer. I mark the tread positions on both stringers from one datum, at the bottom, so they match each other, and lay the two stringers side by side to compare. I check the landing frame sizes against the stringer tops and the building opening. I check that the tread width plus the stringers fits the stair width. If something does not fit, I do not cut. I find where the error is, check the drawing and the site sizes, and raise a query with the supervisor or drawing office before re-marking.
markingPoints: Checks rise, going and number of steps add up
Works out stringer length and angle; full-size check
Marks both stringers from one datum and compares them
Checks treads and landing against stringers and opening
Does not cut if it will not fit; finds error and raises a query

practical1.title: Full-size setting out of a small steel roof truss, with member and gusset marking and a checked record
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a drawing of a small steel roof truss (for example, a span of about 3 m and a rise of about 0.75 m, with angle chords and struts) and enough angle and plate to mark the members and gussets. First, as a group, work out the rafter length and the lengths of the struts, and write them on a calculation sheet. Share the roles: team leader, two setters-out, a marker, and a checker (roles change so every member sets out, marks and checks something). On the plate table or a clean floor, snap the base line, mark the eaves nodes and strike the apex with trammels or a tape, then draw the centre lines and all the nodes. Check the layout: diagonals, both halves equal, and the height. Lay each angle on the layout and mark its cut lines and angles. Make card templates for two gussets straight from the layout and mark them onto plate. Mark each piece with its piece mark. The checker checks every piece against the layout and drawing and fills in the check sheet. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the calculation sheet and check sheet once for the whole group, with the marked pieces.
materials: Truss drawing and blank calculation and check sheets (from the assessor)
Angle lengths (for example 40 × 40 × 5) and 6 mm plate for gussets
Chalk line, soapstone, scriber, trammels, steel tape, steel rule, combination square, sliding bevel
Card for templates, scissors, paint marker
Firm trestles; plate table or clean, flat floor area
photos: The calculation sheet with the rafter and strut lengths worked out
The full-size layout with base line, apex and nodes
The diagonals and height being checked on the layout
An angle laid on the layout with its cut lines marked
Gusset templates and the gussets marked on plate
All marked pieces with piece marks, and the signed check sheet
checklist: Worked out member lengths correctly, or checked them
Set out base line, nodes and centre lines accurately
Checked the layout by diagonals, halves and height
Marked cut lines and angles on members from the layout
Made or marked a gusset from a template taken off the layout
Checked pieces against the layout and recorded results honestly
Handled steel safely and kept the area tidy
safety: Lift long angles with two people and support them on firm trestles
Wear gloves when handling cut steel and safety glasses when punching
Keep scriber and trammel points covered when not in use
Keep walkways clear of steel and chalk lines; follow the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Develop a square-to-round transition by triangulation and mark it out on sheet, with a card check model
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group the sizes of a square-to-round transition (for example, a 300 mm square base, a 200 mm diameter round top and a height of 200 mm, centred). As a group, draw the plan and elevation full size. Divide the circle into 12 equal parts and join the points to the corners of the square. Then find the true length of every line by the right-angled triangle method, and write them in a true-length table. Share the roles: two members draw the plan and true lengths, two build the pattern triangle by triangle from the seam line, and one checks each true length and each triangle against the table (roles change part-way so every member draws and checks). Cut out the pattern in card and bend it to shape to check that it closes and that the top is round and the base square. Correct the pattern if needed. Finally, transfer the pattern onto thin steel sheet (about 1 mm), marking the outline, the seam, the bend lines and the waste side. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the true-length table, the card model and the marked sheet once for the whole group.
materials: Transition sizes and a blank true-length table (from the assessor)
Large sheets of drawing paper or card; pencils, rule, compass, set squares
Thin steel sheet, about 1 mm, large enough for the pattern
Scriber, dividers, steel rule, soapstone or paint marker
Scissors for card; tape to hold the card model
photos: The plan and elevation with the circle divided and lines drawn
The pattern being built triangle by triangle
The card model bent to shape and closed
The pattern marked on steel sheet with bend lines and waste side
The group's check notes beside the finished work
checklist: Drew plan and elevation accurately and divided the circle equally
Found true lengths correctly by the right-angled triangle method
Built the pattern in the right order from the seam
Checked the pattern with a card model and corrected errors
Transferred the pattern to sheet with outline, seam and bend lines
Checked another member's work and recorded it
Worked safely with sheet edges and sharp tools
safety: Wear gloves when handling sheet steel; its edges are sharp
Keep scribers and dividers capped when not in use
Use scissors and knives away from the body
Keep the work area tidy; follow the Centre's rules
